findings.detail: scored 0 — The answer withholds both table values the 0.03 mg/L difference the Benson and Krause basis and the ±0.2 mg/L tolerance comparison and instead picks the EPA table unconditionally rather than advising use of the table matching the governing protocol. Unmet: gives the USGS table value at 20.0 C and 760 mmHg as about 9.09 mg/L; gives the EPA chart value at 20 C and 760 mmHg as about 9.06 mg/L; states the difference is 0.03 mg/L and assesses its significance against the applicable procedure; notes the USGS values are generated from the Benson and Krause equations; compares the 0.03 mg/L difference with the USGS saturation-check tolerance of ±0.2 mg/L; advises using the table belonging to whichever protocol the work is being done under consistently rather than mixing them

scored 0 — The answer gives the two table values and the ~1.0 mg/L drop but it applies the freshwater solubility unchanged to the brackish site (violating a must-not) and it omits the pressure dependence the salinity correction and the caveat that the site-specific split cannot be established from these readings alone. Unmet: states equilibrium saturation also depends on barometric pressure so the site's actual pressure changes the benchmark; states that in brackish water the freshwater value must be reduced by a salinity correction factor before comparison; states the actual warming contribution and remaining drop cannot be established from these readings alone (pressure salinity initial saturation not given)

scored 0 — The answer approves diluting a commercial standard generally and omits the no-dilution rule and the suspension-matrix/nonlinearity explanation violating the 'must not' item against approving dilution of commercial standards other than 4 000-unit formazin. Unmet: states that commercial calibration solutions must not be diluted; gives 4 000-unit formazin as the one exception that may be diluted; explains that diluting changes the suspension matrix so the dilutions are no longer linear

scored 0 — The answer asserts Eh is simply another name for the probe's ORP output and that the millivolt reading is the same numerical value as Eh violating the 'must not' item on interchangeability and it omits the noble-metal/equilibrium definition the reference-electrode caveat and the Eref addition step. Unmet: states that Eh is an equilibrium potential developed at the boundary between a noble-metal electrode and the water and reflects the redox-active species in solution; states that the millivolts the probe reads are not Eh on their own because that raw reading is against the probe's own reference electrode; states that getting Eh means adding the reference electrode's own potential to the measured reading
